newsitem.title: USA: What a long, strange trip it's been.
newsitem.headline: What a long, strange trip it's been.

text.p: By Monday night, Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole's 96-hour campaign marathon had just about run its course. With only a few hours left, highlights and lowlights of the breakneck push began to settle into the foggy memories of participants.
Following is a selection of both. Whether it is a highlight or a lowlight can sometimes be left to the beholder to decide.
-- The Space Centre at Alamogordo, New Mexico. A pretty site for a campaign event, on a hill overlooking the desolate desert with lots of old rockets behind the stage. The weather was nice, too.
-- Airplane hangars. The opposite. Rallies in hangars are noisy, rushed, and set against blue curtains.
-- The Oak Ridge Boys sing "giddayp, giddyap oom papa mau mau" from their country and western hit, "Elvira," at stop after stop, all through the night.
-- Dole's plane gets a flat tire in Houston. Dole, his staff, and the press corps that accompany him commandeer the regular overflow press plane, and chaos breaks out on the tarmac.
-- The Oak Ridge Boys are urged to sing "Elvira" on the jam-packed, commandeered plane, but decline.
-- An $82 hotel room in Sacramento, occupied for 40 minutes. The campaign entourage got a chance to use their rooms for the military-style rest stop of a visit to the bathroom, a shower and a shave.
-- Kennedy, the MTV cable channel hostess and apparent spokeswoman of the unorganized Generation-Xers for Dole, tells a crowd in New Mexico:
"So whether you're young, or old, conservative, or just kind of conservative, get out there tomorrow and vote, encourage everyone you know to vote, or I'll get your goat."

-- Testy encounters at under-secured press platforms between Dole supporters -- venting anti-media hostility that reflected Dole's lambasting of campaign coverage -- and journalists, venting after three nights of catnaps, hectic filing conditions and anti-media hostility.
"Yeah, I'm from the media, screw you," read one popular press corps souvenir button.
-- A local politician in New Mexico, for no discernable reason, estimates turnout at a Dole rally he was addressing at 30,000, at least 15 times a more realistic guess.
-- Hundreds of whooping New Jersey Dole fans jam a diner in the wee hours of the morning, cheer wildly at a mention of the World Series champion New York Yankees, and generally have a ball.

-- "Throat Coat," an herbal tea made of slippery elm bark Dole drinks for his hoarseness. The label sports a New Age message declaring "In this connected universe, we can be active, contributing part of the spirit of nature in its miraculous radiance of purpose, mystery and majesty."

-- Dole licks his lips and rolls his eyes toward the ceiling in anticipation of a chocolate milkshake he ordered at a Dairy Queen he ducked into in Sioux Falls, South Dakota late on Saturday evening. Despite a reputation for dourness, the man can clearly enjoy simple pleasures.
